newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem tells Argentine unions he will never give in.
newsitem.headline: Menem tells Argentine unions he will never give in.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem on Friday told unions threatening another general strike they could walk out for "48 hours or 48 years" but he would still press on with labour reforms reducing their power.
"I will not step aside even if they strike for 48 hours or 48 years. They can die striking, but I will still be here," he said in a speech in the jungle province of Misiones.

The Peronist chief, who faced a 24-hour stoppage in August over tax hikes and benefit cuts and a 36-hour strike last week, has incensed unions with plans to update labour laws and deregulate their lucrative monopoly on health care.
The stand-off became tenser after unions threatened a 48-hour strike on Thursday and Peronism's two prime candidates to succeed Menem in 1999 questioned his reform projects.

Menem has been riding roughshod over union protest, with threats to push the reforms through by decree if Congress puts up a fight. He blamed the resistance to "money interests and leaders who don't want to give up their privileges."
Unions received a health care monopoly from Peronism's founders Juan and Eva Peron in the 1940s. Worth $2.5 billion a year, it is a cash cow they will not surrender without a fight.

Workers face compulsory payments to the union health plan and often a duplicate bill for private health care because of poor service. Menem wants free choice between union plans from next year and open competition with private health care from 1998.

Arguing that modernising labour laws was the only way to get unemployment down from 17.1 percent, Menem wants to dismantle union control on collective wage negotiations, swap redundancy payouts for unemployment insurance, make pay partly dependent on the economic climate and make working hours more flexible.
He tried to kill reports this meant 12-hour work days and workers forced to toil 30 consecutive days without a break.
But the main CGT labour federation's press chief, Carlos West Ocampo, summed up union sentiment: "Flexibility equals lower salaries and the dehumanization of work."

Peronist politicians sympathised. Party second-in-command Eduardo Duhalde, governor of Buenos Aires province and 1999 hopeful, said his followers in Congress would not pass any bill making pay variable or setting a 12-hour workday.
"These are times we should be working less hours, not more, to help the unemployed find work," said Duhalde.
His main rival for 1999, former Tucuman governor Ramon "Palito" Ortega, said it was "worrying we are accepting modernisation of labour laws that alter workers' acquired rights."
